messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kaito had always been drawn to the stage, his body a fluid expression of emotion and movement. As a dancer, he was used to channeling his feelings into performance. But nothing could have prepared him for the emotional toll of working as a relief worker in a war zone. The memories of that time still lingered, refusing to be choreographed away. It started with the smell of alcohol, a scent that transported him back to the makeshift medical tent where he had witnessed unimaginable suffering. The same smell would waft through the dance studio, and suddenly Kaito would be reliving the event - the sounds, the screams, the feeling of helplessness. His mind would flash back to the moment when, in a desperate attempt to save lives, he had acted in ways that went against his values as a healer. The shame would wash over him like a wave, leaving him breathless and disoriented. But it wasn't just the smell of alcohol that triggered these episodes. The time of day also played a cruel trick on Kaito's mind. Whenever the sun began to set at the same hour as the event had occurred, he could feel his anxiety spiking. His heart would start racing, and before he knew it, he was back in the war zone, reliving every terrifying moment. The memories themselves were not just painful recollections; they felt like a living, breathing entity that haunted Kaito's every waking moment. He couldn't shake off the feeling that his reactions since the event showed him to be a lousy coper. Every flashback, every nightmare, seemed to reinforce this notion - that he was weak, that he couldn't rely on himself. As these negative appraisals took hold, they began to shape Kaito's behavior in subtle but insidious ways. He started avoiding certain dance moves, the ones that required him to be still for a moment, because it reminded him of the frozen moments during the event when time seemed to stand still. He would avoid performances at night, fearing the familiar dread that crept over him as the sun dipped below the horizon. But the memories were relentless, and they began to shape Kaito's perception of his surroundings in ways he couldn't control. The smell of burnt offerings from a nearby street vendor would suddenly become the acrid scent of burning buildings, transporting him back to the war zone. His mind was constantly on high alert, waiting for the next trigger that would set off another flashback. Kaito had tried to push through these episodes, to power through his performances as if nothing was wrong. But it was taking a toll on his marriage, his relationships with colleagues, and most of all, his own sense of self-worth. He couldn't shake off the feeling that he was losing himself in the process, that the memories were slowly devouring him whole. It was only when Kaito realized that he couldn't continue living like this, constantly on edge, that he sought help. He hoped to find a way to quiet the memories, to silence the negative voices that had taken up residence in his mind. Most of all, he yearned for a sense of peace, one that would allow him to reclaim his stage, his body, and his life.
